title: Use the quality checklist as a review tool
lead: Connect concerns to architectural controls, ownership, and observable evidence.
bullets: System and process concerns both matter in ML-intensive systems.
Select relevant checks rather than treating a short list as the entire checklist.
Map each concern to a control, owner, and evidence.
Keep limits visible: the separate corrigendum remains unread.
example: Completeness validation addresses input quality; it is not by itself evidence of SS5 cyberattack defense.
takeaway: A checklist supports structured review; it is not a certification claim.

title: Predictive quality and system performance
lead: Choose an acceptable model and system from several quality objectives.
bullets: Accuracy alone is an incomplete objective, especially with imbalanced outcomes.
Performance includes the end-to-end deadline and resource use.
Complexity must justify training and operating costs.
Acceptance depends on the task and the consequences of errors.
example: A heavier churn model is useful only if its quality benefit justifies cost and still meets the campaign’s deadline.
takeaway: Define acceptance criteria before selecting a more complex model.

title: Robustness: invalid, unfamiliar, or ordinary?
lead: Different inputs need different responses; do not treat every unusual value as the same failure.
bullets: Contract validity and model applicability are distinct.
OOD inputs may be structurally valid but poorly represented in training.
Confidence alone is not a guaranteed detector of unfamiliar inputs.
Fallbacks must be validated for the intended situation.
example: A missing activity value is invalid; a new customer population may be valid but outside the model’s reliable coverage.
takeaway: An architecture needs an explicit response when the model should not be trusted.

title: Explainability and auditability differ
lead: Explaining feature influence and reconstructing a historical decision are complementary tasks.
bullets: Explanation helps interpret model behavior in context.
Auditability needs historical evidence and traceable versions.
Decision review includes business policy and action, not only the model.
Limits: SHAP and LIME do not prove causality or fairness.
example: An engagement contribution may help explain Ana’s score; it cannot prove why she would leave the bank.
takeaway: Protect evidence and test whether authorized reviewers can actually retrieve it.

title: Fairness: prediction versus treatment
lead: Name what is being compared before selecting a metric or declaring an improvement.
bullets: Prediction fairness: compare errors or calibration across relevant groups.
Treatment fairness: inspect access to offers and policy effects.
Context: select targets based on harms and requirements.
Trade-offs: one metric does not settle every fairness concern.
example: Equal churn prediction errors do not imply equal access to retention offers under campaign allocation rules.
takeaway: Keep predictive quality and the consequences of intervention distinct.
